Polynomial Separation of a Shared Tensor Leg and Matrix Multiplication in Arbitrary Characteristic

Houxi Lü

October 9, 2026

**Abstract**

We improve the shared-leg separation construction in Proposition 3.1 of OpenAI, _An Upper Bound of_ 9/4 _for the Matrix Multiplication Exponent_ (October 2, 2026). If _M_ tensor blocks have a common first space and independent matched sectors on their other two spaces, then _M+n_-1 copies of their matched sum degenerate to the full direct sum of the blocks, each tensored with an _n_-dimensional dot product. For _n=M_, this reduces the number of source copies from 5_M_ to 2_M_-1. The construction uses polynomial interpolation and truncated local substitution, with no roots of unity or factorial denominators. It works over every field containing enough distinct elements. We verify that the remaining spectral and discrete-growth arguments of the cited preprint are independent of characteristic. Over an algebraic closure, the replacement therefore gives \(\omega\le 9/4\) in every characteristic.

## 1 The replacement and its setting

The separation problem is to make each block read its own copy of a shared input. In Proposition 3.1 of OpenAI [1], this is done by Fourier projection followed by a weight degeneration. We use evaluation of polynomials instead. Evaluation at _M_ distinct points gives _M_ independent input coordinates; a local substitution allows us to approach this evaluation map through restrictions of ordinary polynomial multiplication.

We follow the notation of the cited paper: \(A=\sum_hA_h\) denotes a matched sum, \(A\ge B\) means that _B_ is a restriction of _A_, \(\otimes\) denotes tensor product, and \(A^{\oplus r}\) denotes a full direct sum of _r_ copies. An integer _r_ also denotes the direct sum of _r_ scalar tensors, so \(A\otimes r\cong A^{\oplus r}\). All spaces are finite-dimensional over a algebraically closed field _F_. Tensors are viewed as trilinear forms, and a restriction pulls a form back along a linear map on each of its three spaces.

We use \(\unknown\) for an algebraic degeneration: the three pullback maps may have entries in \(F[\varepsilon,\varepsilon^{-1}]\), provided that the resulting form is polynomial in \(\varepsilon\); its value at \(\varepsilon=0\) is the target tensor. This extends the fixed-substitution, monomial-weight convention of Section 2.2 of the cited paper. Its interpolation argument still applies. Indeed, if the resulting polynomial family has degree _L_ and constant term _B_, interpolation of its _j_th tensor power at _jL_+1 distinct nonzero points gives

\((jL+1)\lambda(A)^j\ge\lambda(B)^j.\)

Over an infinite field, taking _j_th roots proves degeneration monotonicity for every tensor character \(\lambda\).

## 2 Separation by polynomial multiplication

**Proposition 2.1** (Shared-leg separation)**.** _Let_ \(M,n\ge 1\)_, and suppose that F contains at least M+n_-1 _distinct elements. Let_<tbc>

\(A_h:X\times Y_h\times Z_h\longrightarrow F(1\le h\le M)\)

<tbc>_be trilinear forms, and define their matched sum by_<tbc>

\(A(x,y,z)=\sum_{h=1}^MA_h(x,y_h,z_h),y\in\oplus_hY_h,z\in\oplus_hZ_h.\)

<tbc>_Then_

\(\boxed{A^{\oplus(M+n-1)}\unknown\rightarrow\oplus_{h=1}^M(A_h\otimes B_X(n)).}\) (2.1)

_Here B<sub>X</sub>(n_) _is the dot-product tensor_

\(B_X(n):F\times J\times J^\vee\longrightarrow F,(c,j,\varphi)\longmapsto c\varphi(j),\)

_for any n-dimensional space J. The direct sum on the right of_ (2.1) _has independent spaces on all three legs._

_Proof._ We want the _h_th block to read only the _h_th copy of _X_. Polynomial interpolation provides exactly such coordinates. Choose distinct \(a_1,\dots,a_M\in F\) and put<tbc>

\(P=F[t]_{<M},J=F[u]/(u^n),\)

<tbc>where _F_\[_t_\]_<sub>\<d</sub>_ denotes the polynomials of degree less than _d_. The map

\(e:P\longrightarrow F^M,p\longmapsto(p(a_1),\dots,p(a_M))\) (2.2)

is an isomorphism: a polynomial of degree less than _M_ cannot vanish at all _M_ points unless it is zero, and the dimensions agree. Thus \(X\otimes P\) can supply the desired independent copies of _X_.

For each _h_, substitute \(t=a_h+\varepsilon u\) and define<tbc>

\(\sigma_h(p,j)=p(a_h+\varepsilon u)j\text{in}J[\varepsilon].\)

<tbc>The substitution is defined on all of _F_\[_t_\]; in particular, \(\sigma_h\) is bilinear on \(P\times J\). It has two useful properties. At \(\varepsilon=0\) it becomes \(\sigma_h(p,j)=p(a_h)j\), which reads exactly the evaluation coordinate in (2.2). For \(\varepsilon\neq 0\), substitution identifies _F_\[_t_\]_<sub>\<n</sub>_ with _J_:

\((t-a_h)^s\longmapsto\varepsilon^su^s(0\le s<n).\)

Both sides are bases, and all the displayed factors are invertible.

We now assemble these actions into one polynomial family on<tbc>

\(\widetilde{X}=X\otimes P,\widetilde{Y}=\oplus_h(Y_h\otimes J),\widetilde{Z}=\oplus_h(Z_h\otimes J^\vee).\)

<tbc>Define \(\Phi(\varepsilon)\) on matching components by

\(\Phi(\varepsilon)(x\otimes p,y_h\otimes j,z_h\otimes\varphi)=A_h(x,y_h,z_h)\varphi(\sigma_h(p,j)),\) (2.3)

and set it to zero on components with different _Y_ - and _Z_-labels. Extend by trilinearity. Each coefficient is polynomial in \(\varepsilon\). We will obtain this family by restricting _M+n_-1 copies of _A_. Put \(\ell=M+n-1\), _Q=F[t]\_ and \(W=F[t]_{<\ell}\). Let \(\mu:P\otimes Q\longrightarrow W,\mu(p,q)=pq\) be ordinary multiplication, and let \(C_\mu(p,q,\psi)=\psi(pq)(p\in P,q\in Q,\psi\in W^\vee)\) be its trilinear form. For each _h_, define \(g_h:Q\longrightarrow J[\varepsilon],q\longmapsto q(a_h+\varepsilon u),\iota_h:W\longrightarrow J[\varepsilon],f\longmapsto f(a_h+\varepsilon u).\) Here and below maps with polynomial coefficients are extended linearly over the parameter ring when composed. Substitution preserves products, so \(\sigma_h\circ(\mathrm{id}_P\otimes g_h)=\iota_h\circ\mu.\) (2.4) This is the relation that connects our family to ordinary multiplication. Work temporarily over \(F[\varepsilon,\varepsilon^{-1}]\), so that _gh_ is invertible. Pull back \(A\otimes C_\mu\) along the three maps \(\alpha=\mathrm{id}_{X\otimes P},\)
\(\beta=\oplus_h(\mathrm{id}_{Y_h}\otimes g_h^{-1}),\)
\(\gamma=\oplus_h(\mathrm{id}_{Z_h}\otimes\iota_h^\vee).\) The maps on the last two legs take \(\widetilde{Y}\) to \(\oplus_h(Y_h\otimes Q)\) and \(\widetilde{Z}\) to \(\oplus_h(Z_h\otimes W^\vee)\), respectively. On the _h_th component, the auxiliary pairing becomes \((\iota_h^\vee\varphi)(\mu(p,g_h^{-1}j))=\varphi(\sigma_h(p,j))\) by (2.4). Hence the pullback is precisely \(\Phi(\varepsilon)\), including its zero terms on unmatched components. It remains to pay for \(C_\mu\). Choose \(\ell\) distinct points \(b_1,\dots,b_\ell\in F\). Evaluation at these points identifies _W_ with \(F^\ell\). Multiplication in _W_ can therefore be computed by evaluating the two inputs, multiplying their values at the \(\ell\) points, and interpolating the output. Thus \(\ell\ge C_\mu,A^{\oplus\ell}\cong A\otimes\ell\ge A\otimes C_\mu.\) Composing this fixed restriction with \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\) gives Laurent-polynomial pullback maps from \(A^{\oplus\ell}\) whose result is the polynomial family \(\Phi(\varepsilon)\). Finally, at \(\varepsilon=0\), equation (2.3) reads \(\Phi(0)(x\otimes p,y_h\otimes j,z_h\otimes\varphi)=p(a_h)A_h(x,y_h,z_h)\varphi(j).\) Under \(\mathrm{id}_X\otimes e:X\otimes P\cong\oplus_hX\), the _h_th block reads only the _h_th copy of _X_. Its other two spaces are already separate. Consequently \(\Phi(0)\cong\oplus_h(A_h\otimes B_X(n)),\) which proves the degeneration. The construction uses no roots of unity and no division by factorials. The inverse of _gh_ is simply \(j(u)\mapsto j((t-a_h)/\varepsilon)\), using the representative of degree less than _n_ in _J_. In particular, its Laurent-polynomial form is valid in every characteristic. The family \(\Phi\) has degree at most min(_M_-1_,n_-1) in \(\varepsilon\), since powers _un_ and higher vanish in _J_.

## 3 The spectral comparison

Let _F_ now be infinite, and let \(\lambda\) be a tensor character in the sense of Section 2 of the cited paper: it is normalized, restriction-monotone, additive on full direct sums, and multiplicative on tensor products. Write \(\lambda(B_X(n))=n^{p_X}\), with \(p_X\in[0,1]\), as in its Section 2.1. Proposition 2.1 and interpolation monotonicity give

\((M+n-1)\lambda(A)\ge n^{p_X}\sum_h\lambda(A_h).\) (3.1)

Taking _n=M_ yields

\((2M-1)\lambda(A)\ge M^{p_X}\sum_h\lambda(A_h).\) (3.2)

This replaces the factor 5_M_ in Proposition 3.1 of the cited paper.

The proof of its Corollary 3.2 now goes through with this new factor. To see precisely what changes, let \(T=\sum_iT_i\) be a matched sum and let _q_ be a rational probability vector. In \(T^{\otimes N}\) retain only sector words containing _Nq<sub>i</sub>_ copies of label _i_. There are<tbc>

\(M_N=\frac{N!}{\prod_i(Nq_i)!}\)

<tbc>blocks, each of character value \(\prod_i\lambda(T_i)^{Nq_i}\). Equation (3.2) gives<tbc>

\(\lambda(T)\ge\left(\frac{M_N}{2M_N-1}\right)^{1/N}M_N^{p_X/N}\prod_i\lambda(T_i)^{q_i}.\)

<tbc>The first factor tends to 1, while log_M<sub>N</sub>/N_ tends to the entropy \(H(q)=-\sum_iq_ilogq_i\). By continuity in _q_, we recover exactly the original shared-leg inequality

\(\lambda(T)\ge e^{p_XH(q)}\prod_i\lambda(T_i)^{q_i}.\) (3.3)

The factorials here count words as integers; they are not inverted in _F_. The improved finite copy count therefore preserves the entropy exponent. By itself it does not give a strict improvement below 9/4.

## 4 The consequence in positive characteristic

The new separation argument works over every infinite field. To apply the remainder of the cited paper in positive characteristic, we need to check its other field-dependent steps. We record these checks rather than repeat its proofs.

First, the rank bound for polynomial multiplication follows from interpolation at distinct points, which is valid over any infinite field. Second, the determinant filtration in its Lemma 4.1 uses

\(0\longrightarrow(uw-vs)V_{e-1}\longrightarrow V_e\otimes span(s,w)\longrightarrow V_{e+1}\longrightarrow 0.\)

Here _V<sub>e</sub>_ is the space of homogeneous degree-_e_ forms in _u,v_, and the last map substitutes (_s,w_)=(_u,v_). It is surjective on monomials. Multiplication by _uw-vs_ is injective, and its image has the dimension of the kernel. These facts hold in every characteristic, including 2. Multiplication by a first input preserves this kernel, so the block degeneration in that lemma also holds without a characteristic assumption.

Third, the three-sector construction in its Lemma 4.2 only uses coordinate restrictions, basis permutations, and integer weights of a degeneration parameter. It does not divide by 3: the uniform probability vector and its entropy are real numbers used to compare character values. Finally, the detecting-character proof in its Appendix A uses the ordered tensor semiring, flattening ranks, finite-dimensional real separation, compactness, and a fixed-point theorem. Every nonzero tensor still restricts to a scalar tensor over an arbitrary field, and all semiring and rank comparisons used there remain valid. The separation and fixed-point arguments concern real-valued states, not the characteristic of the tensor field.

These observations justify using Sections 4 and 5 and Appendix A of the cited paper over an algebraically closed field _F_ of any characteristic, with Proposition 2.1 in place of its Proposition 3.1. For clarity, the resulting chain of inequalities is as follows. Put<tbc>

\(t=(p_X+p_Y+p_Z)/3>0,C(a,b)=\sum_{i=0}^{a-1}\sum_{j=0}^{b-1}x_iy_jz_{i+j},\)

<tbc>and use the original symmetrized profile<tbc>

\(P(a,b)=\left(\prod_{\pi\in S_3}\lambda_\pi(C(a,b))\right)^{1/(6t)}.\)

<tbc>Its concavity and shifted tripling follow from the two constructions just checked and (3.3). The real argument of Lemma 5.1 then gives

\(a^{4/3}\le P(a,a)\le(2a-1)^{1/t}.\)

Consequently \(t\le 3/4\), and every character satisfies \(\lambda(T_d)\le d^{9/4}\) for the matrix multiplication tensor \(T_d=\sum_{i,j,k=1}^dx_{ij}y_{jk}z_{ki}\).

Write \(\nu=inf_{d\ge 2}log_dR(T_d)\), again as in the cited paper. Its detecting-character lemma, applied with \(k=\lceil d^\nu\rceil-1\), yields

\(d^\nu\le d^{9/4}+1.\)

Letting \(d\rightarrow\infty\) gives \(\nu\le 9/4\). The recursive bilinear-algorithm argument in its proof of Theorem 1.1 therefore gives \(\omega_F\le 9/4\).

**Corollary 4.1.** _For every algebraically closed field K, the matrix multiplication exponent satisfies_ \(\omega_K\le 9/4\)_. In particular, the bound holds in all but finitely many characteristics; in fact no characteristic needs to be excluded._
